line: e4 c5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 g6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nf6
teaches: Against a fianchettoed bishop you can either spend a quiet move keeping the position intact, or resolve the centre at once and accept a structural change in return. The quiet move looks like it does nothing and is preventing something; the exchange gives the defender doubled pawns and gives up the tension. Both are real; they are not the same game.
explains: Both sides are developed and the tension in the centre still stands. One try is a modest pawn move on the edge that removes a square before it is used. The other takes on c6 immediately, doubling the pawns there and opening a file, which changes what both sides are playing for.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 g6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nf6 a3
teaches: A pawn move on the edge that develops nothing and attacks nothing can still be the best move on the board. Judge it by the square it takes away: if the piece that wanted that square was going to arrive with tempo, the quiet move has saved the move it would have cost you.
explains: The pawn steps to a3 and covers b4, which is the square the queen and the dark-squared bishop both eye when they want to hit the knight on c3 with something behind it. Nothing is threatened and nothing is developed; what has changed is that a whole family of annoying moves is off the board before it appears.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 g6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nf6 a3 O-O Bc4
teaches: A bishop aimed at f7 is doing two jobs whenever the defender has castled: it hits the pawn in front of the king, and it covers the square in the centre that the defender's pieces most want. Before you decide the bishop is only an attacking piece, look at what it holds behind the attack.
explains: The bishop comes to c4 and stares at the pawn on f7, which is the only pawn near the king not defended by another pawn. From the same square it covers d5, so the freeing pawn break in the centre is contested before it is played. That double duty is why this square, rather than a more modest one, is the one to aim for. It also answers the tempting grab in the centre: the pawn there is defended once and attacked once, so taking it is not winning a pawn — it is a trade that banks on the pawn push which would fork the recapturing knight and this bishop, and the bishop on c4 is the piece that break has to get past.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 g6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nf6 a3 O-O Bc4 Nxe4
teaches: Given a chance to win back a piece or to take a pawn with check, look at what the check does to the defender's position before assuming the recapture is better. A capture that forces the king to move or drags a rook onto an awkward square buys more than the exchange of pieces it costs.
explains: The knight has taken on e4 and there are two ways to answer. Recapturing the knight straight away keeps everything simple. Taking on f7 with check first is the move: the king has to choose between stepping out and letting the rook come to f7, and only then does the knight come off. Material ends up level — what has changed is where the black king lives.

line: e4 c5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 g6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Bg7 Be3 Nf6 Nxc6 bxc6 e5
teaches: After trading in the centre, the follow-up push earns its place if it hits a piece and takes a square in one move. The knight it attacks is usually the piece holding the defender's position together, and the square behind the pawn is where the attack wants to land next.
explains: Black's pawn stands on c6 with b7 and c7 empty behind it. The pawn advances to e5, hitting the knight on f6, and it covers d6 as well, so the knight cannot drop back into the middle of the position. It has to go somewhere awkward, and every move it spends finding a square is a move the attacker spends developing.
